hook: The king of Mali whose gold-laden pilgrimage made him a legend.

pages.x: Musa became mansa, or king, of Mali around 1312. His empire stretched 2,000 km across West Africa, from the Atlantic coast to Timbuktu and Gao, and held rich gold fields at a time when gold from West Africa filled the treasuries of Europe and the Middle East.
Musa told an Egyptian official that he became king because the mansa before him had sailed into the Atlantic with 2,000 ships to find the far side of the ocean, and never came back.

In 1324 he set off for Mecca with a vast caravan, said to number 60,000 people, among them 12,000 servants dressed in silk, and camels carrying tonnes of gold. It was one of the most talked-about journeys of the age.

pages.t: He crashed the price of gold
pages.x: Passing through Cairo, he gave away and spent so much gold that its value in Egypt fell for years afterwards. On the way home he even had to borrow money at a high rate of interest.

He came home with scholars and an architect from Muslim Spain, who is said to have built the Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu, of mud brick and wood. Timbuktu became a great centre of Islamic learning, with libraries of thousands of manuscripts.

In 1375 a map made in Majorca, the Catalan Atlas, showed Mansa Musa enthroned in the middle of Africa, wearing a crown and holding up a golden nugget: Europe's picture of the richest king in the world.

Mansa Musa is often called the richest person in history, though his wealth is impossible to measure. His pilgrimage put Mali on the map of the world, and his support for learning made Timbuktu famous for centuries.
pts: Ruled the Mali Empire at its height
Made the most famous pilgrimage to Mecca
Made Timbuktu a centre of learning
Called the richest man in history
